record.title: CART reports adaptive red teaming finds failures missed by static prompt replay
record.summary: The CART preprint presents closed-loop red teaming in which a Challenger adapts probes using earlier results while a separate Judge scores the evidence. Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores than direct replay of seed prompts for targets with available baselines. The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; static replay uses the same Judge and rubric. Budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier and JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. The paper reports the largest gap on tool-mediated Agentic cases and says observed test-volume share is not a measure of real-world failure prevalence. The result supports adaptive testing as a way to expose benchmark-conditioned weaknesses, not a claim that deployed models fail at the observed rates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: CART uses a closed-loop Challenger–Target–Judge design in which findings from earlier rounds guide later probe selection and adaptation, while retaining probe lineage and scoring records.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores with adaptive testing than direct replay of stored seed prompts for targets with available baselines; the largest separation is reported in Agentic evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge, and static replay uses the same Gemini Judge and scoring rubric; per-run budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier/JAH and 3,200 for Agentic.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper states that observed test-volume share is not real-world failure prevalence, capabilities and test sets differ across conditions, and Judge/Challenger pairing and risk-score calibration affect which evidence is found.

evidence_gaps.description: The adaptive-versus-static comparisons have not been independently reproduced with repeated seeds and independent probe generators or judges.
Adaptive and static probes can differ in capability coverage and difficulty, and the paper's composite risk score is not independently calibrated to real-world harm.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper's benchmark-scoped result generalizes, adaptive probe generation can reveal failures missed by static seed replay and change how red-team budgets are allocated for frontier models and tool-using agents. The result does not measure real-world failure rates.
limitations: Results are paper-reported and depend on the selected Challenger, Judge, prompts, budgets, seed sets and scoring rubric; no independent replication was performed.
Observed test-volume share and failure rates are not real-world prevalence estimates. Adaptive and static conditions can exercise different capabilities and test difficulty.
Risk scores are LLM-Judge dependent. The paper reports stronger peer agreement on binary verdicts than on rationales and score calibration.
Each Challenger–Judge interaction cell in the role matrix is one aggregate run, so interaction effects are not separated from run-level randomness.
Larger seed banks, taxonomies and budgets increase retrieval, inference and validation costs.
brief.summary: The CART preprint presents closed-loop red teaming in which a Challenger adapts probes using earlier results while a separate Judge scores the evidence. Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores than direct replay of seed prompts for targets with available baselines. The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; static replay uses the same Judge and rubric. Budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier and JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. The paper reports the largest gap on tool-mediated Agentic cases and says observed test-volume share is not a measure of real-world failure prevalence. The result supports adaptive testing as a way to expose benchmark-conditioned weaknesses, not a claim that deployed models fail at the observed rates.

technical.claimed_result: On Frontier and JAH suites (1,000-round per-run budgets) and an Agentic suite (3,200 rounds), adaptive testing reports higher failure rates and average risk scores than replaying stored seed prompts for available targets. The largest separation occurs in Agentic cases. In a separate 282-judgment peer audit, six independent peers agree on binary verdicts 98.9% of the time, while rationales and risk-score calibration are less stable.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint defines the framework, evaluation data families, comparison protocol, scoring roles and author-reported results. No independent reproduction was conducted; the results remain claims from the paper.
technical.mechanism: CART separates a Challenger that creates or adapts probes, a Target that responds or acts, and a Judge that assesses evidence. It stores results and lineage and uses earlier findings to direct later testing under a fixed budget, with diversity controls to reduce repetitive probes.
technical.novelty: Adapts red-team probes during a fixed-budget run based on observed weaknesses while preserving lineage and separating generation, target response and judgment; contrasts this closed-loop search with direct benchmark seed replay.
technical.regime: Paper evaluations on three families: Frontier curated risk cases, JAH harmful/refusal/multistep benchmark cases, and Agentic cases involving tools, retrieved content, state and multistep actions. 1,000 rounds each for Frontier/JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. Targets include seven named model families. Results are observed under the authors' prompts, budgets, Judge, Challenger and risk rubric.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes probe lineage, run budgets, random seeds, complete call logs and peer audits; the public preprint is inspectable. the research desk did not reproduce the experiments. Some role-comparison cells are one aggregate run, and the paper does not establish real-world prevalence.
technical.strongest_baseline: Direct replay of stored seed prompts, evaluated with the same Gemini Judge and rubric as CART. The main comparison fixes Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; a separate Frontier-family experiment varies these roles. This controls evaluator identity for the static/adaptive comparison but does not establish that LLM-judged risk scores are ground truth.

brief.title: CART reports adaptive red teaming finds failures missed by static prompt replay
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported comparison holds, fixed benchmark prompts can understate weaknesses that appear when the test context adapts to earlier model behavior. Adaptive, provenance-tracked probes could change how model and agent evaluations allocate a fixed test budget. The paper's results are Judge- and setup-dependent and do not estimate real-world failure prevalence.
